title: Decision Theory
description: How to choose well when outcomes are uncertain: expected value, utility and risk, decision trees, the value of information, updating beliefs, and where real choosers depart from the theory.
audience: A capable adult comfortable with percentages and simple probability. They have met conditional probability and expected value and some basic game theory, and want a working method for real choices.
outcomes: You'll be able to lay a choice out as options, states and payoffs and compare options by expected value.
You'll be able to roll back a decision tree to the best first move.
You'll be able to compute a certainty equivalent and say what a utility curve implies about risk.
You'll be able to update a probability with Bayes' rule and price information before buying it.
You'll be able to name the main ways real choices depart from expected utility.

modules.title: Choosing with numbers
modules.summary: Lay a choice out as options, states and payoffs, then use probability to compare options by expected value, in a table or a tree, and see what to do when no probabilities are known.

modules.title: Value and risk
modules.summary: Money is a poor measure of value. Utility explains why a sure thing can beat a better average, and gives risk attitudes an exact meaning.

modules.title: Information and belief
modules.summary: Update probabilities with Bayes' rule, then price the information itself: what it is worth to learn the state before choosing.

modules.title: Real choosers and other choosers
modules.summary: Where people depart from expected utility, and what changes when the other side of the table is a player and not the weather.

lessons.title: Options, states and payoffs
lessons.objective: Lay a choice out as a table of options, states and payoffs, and remove any option that another option beats in every state.

concepts.title: State of the world
concepts.summary: A way things might turn out that you do not control and cannot choose, such as 'it rains' or 'demand is high'.

concepts.title: Payoff
concepts.summary: The value, in one stated unit, of choosing a given option when a given state turns out to hold.

concepts.title: Dominance
concepts.summary: Option X dominates option Y when X pays at least as much as Y in every state and strictly more in at least one.

misconceptions: Treating an option that wins in one state as dominating; dominance needs every state.
Mixing up what the chooser controls (options) with what they do not (states), so that a state is listed as a choice.
Counting the option with the single largest payoff as best, ignoring how it does elsewhere.
sequence: Open on a three-by-three table of payoffs for launching a product in a boom, flat or slump market.
Name the three parts: options are rows, states are columns, each cell is a payoff in one unit.
Compare two rows cell by cell to find dominance, and show a pair where neither dominates.
Remove the dominated option and note that the choice is unchanged by doing so.
Close on the limit: after dominance is used up, options still disagree, which needs probabilities.
examples: Payoffs in thousands of dollars across Boom, Flat, Slump. A: 50, 30, 10. B: 40, 30, 5. C: 80, 20, -20. A beats B in Boom (50 > 40) and Slump (10 > 5) and ties in Flat (30 = 30), so A dominates B. C beats A in Boom only, so neither dominates the other.

figures.shows: The three-by-three payoff table, with rows and columns labelled by option and state. Only the table; the dominated row is not marked.
figures.learnerAction: Tap two rows to compare them cell by cell; each cell turns green, grey or red as the first row beats, ties or loses to the second.

questionPlan.sample: Using the table, which option is dominated by another?
In how many states does A pay strictly more than B?
Option Z pays 60, 25, 10 in Boom, Flat, Slump. Does Z dominate A (50, 30, 10)?
questionPlan.answer: No: it pays less in Flat
choices: No: it pays less in Flat

lessons.title: Expected value
lessons.objective: Compute the expected value of a gamble and use it to choose between a gamble and a sure amount.

concepts.title: Expected value
concepts.summary: The sum over outcomes of probability times payoff; the average payoff over many repetitions.

concepts.title: Net payoff
concepts.summary: The payoff after subtracting what the option costs to take.

misconceptions: Reading expected value as the outcome you expect to see; a single play of a gamble almost never pays its expected value.
Forgetting to subtract the stake, so a ticket costing $5 with an expected prize of $6 looks like a $6 gain rather than a $1 gain.
Averaging the payoffs without weighting by probability.
sequence: Start from a gamble with three prizes and weights and compute 0.2 × 100 + 0.5 × 40 + 0.3 × (-10).
Check the probabilities sum to 1 before multiplying anything.
Interpret the result as a long-run average and run it for a thousand plays in the simulator.
Subtract the price of entry to get net expected value, then compare with a sure alternative.
Work the European roulette bet to show a small negative expectation that is real but hidden in any one play.
examples: Gamble: 20% chance of 100, 50% of 40, 30% of -10. EV = 20 + 20 - 3 = 37. A ticket costs $5 and pays $20 with probability 0.3, otherwise nothing: EV of the prize = 6, net = 6 - 5 = 1. European roulette single-number bet, stake 1: wins 35 with probability 1/37, loses 1 with probability 36/37, EV = 35/37 - 36/37 = -1/37 ≈ -0.027.

figures.shows: A probability-weighted bar chart of the gamble's three prizes, and a running average of simulated plays settling towards the EV line. The EV figure is not printed.
figures.learnerAction: Press play to simulate 1, 10, 100 and 1000 plays and watch the average.
figures.placement: Why EV is a long-run average.

questionPlan.sample: A gamble pays 100 with probability 0.2, 40 with probability 0.5 and -10 with probability 0.3. What is its expected value?
A ticket costing $5 pays $20 with probability 0.3 and nothing otherwise. What is the net expected gain per ticket, in dollars?
A single-number bet at European roulette stakes 1 and pays 35 on a win, with 37 pockets. What is the expected net gain per unit staked, to three decimal places?

lessons.title: Decision trees
lessons.objective: Draw a decision tree with decision and chance nodes and roll it back to the best first move.

concepts.title: Decision node
concepts.summary: A point in the tree where the chooser picks a branch.

concepts.title: Chance node
concepts.summary: A point where nature picks a branch with stated probabilities.

concepts.title: Rolling back
concepts.summary: Working from the leaves to the root, replacing each chance node by its expected value and each decision node by its best branch.

misconceptions: Rolling back from the root rather than the leaves, which fixes values that depend on later choices.
Putting the probabilities of a later chance node on the first branch, so that they are multiplied in twice.
Choosing the branch with the biggest single leaf instead of the biggest rolled-back value.
sequence: Show one decision with two options and one chance node under the first.
Write each leaf as a net payoff so costs are paid on the path that incurs them.
Roll back: chance node becomes the sum of probability times value, decision node becomes the larger branch.
Extend the tree by one more chance node to show that rollback works from the end.
Read off the whole plan, not only the first move: what to do if each state occurs.
examples: Outdoor stall: costs 200 to enter, takes 900 in sun (probability 0.6) or 300 in rain (probability 0.4). Net: 700 and 100. EV = 0.6 × 700 + 0.4 × 100 = 420 + 40 = 460. Indoor market pays 400 for sure, so choose the stall. Two-stage tree: option A pays 100 with probability 0.5, otherwise reaches a node that pays 200 with probability 0.4 and 0 with probability 0.6 (value 80); A = 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × 80 = 90. Option B is a sure 85, so A wins by 5.

figures.shows: A decision tree with a square decision node, circular chance nodes, branch probabilities and net payoffs at the leaves. Node values are left blank.
figures.learnerAction: Tap each node, from the leaves back to the root, to enter its value; the tree checks it and fills it in.

questionPlan.sample: Stall tree: 0.6 chance of net 700, 0.4 chance of net 100. What is the value of the chance node?
A sure 400 against the stall tree (value 460). Which first move does the plan choose?
Option A pays 100 with probability 0.5, otherwise a second gamble: 200 with probability 0.4, 0 with probability 0.6. What is A's value?

lessons.title: When no probabilities are known
lessons.objective: Apply maximin, maximax and minimax regret to a payoff table and see why they can disagree.

concepts.title: Maximin
concepts.summary: Choose the option whose worst payoff is largest.

concepts.title: Regret
concepts.summary: In a given state, the best payoff available in that state minus the payoff you got.

concepts.title: Minimax regret
concepts.summary: Choose the option whose largest regret across states is smallest.

misconceptions: Believing the rules must agree if the table is fair; they answer different questions and often disagree.
Computing regret against the best option overall and not against the best in each state.
Treating maximin as always cautious and therefore always right, when it can reject an option that wins heavily in nearly every state.
sequence: Return to the payoff table, now saying the probabilities are simply not known.
Maximax and maximin as the optimist's and the pessimist's rules.
Build the regret table column by column: subtract each payoff from the column's best.
Show that maximin and minimax regret pick different options on the same table.
Name the cost: every rule hides an implicit view of the probabilities, so ask what is known before choosing a rule.
examples: Payoffs in Boom, Flat, Slump. A: 50, 30, 10. C: 80, 20, -20. D: 40, 40, 35. Worst cases 10, -20, 35, so maximin picks D. Column bests are 80, 40, 35. Regrets: A = 30, 10, 25 (max 30); C = 0, 20, 55 (max 55); D = 40, 0, 0 (max 40). Minimax regret picks A. Maximax picks C (80).

figures.shows: The payoff table with a switch for payoffs, worst cases and regrets. Only the rule chosen is shown.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the rules and tap the option each rule would pick.

questionPlan.sample: Which option does maximin choose (A, C or D)?
What is C's largest regret across the three states?
Which option does minimax regret choose (A, C or D)?

historyNotes: Laplace's principle of insufficient reason, giving equal weight to every state, is the older answer to unknown probabilities; see unverified for the dates of Wald and Savage.

lessons.title: Utility and the St Petersburg problem
lessons.objective: Explain why expected money can mislead and compute expected utility with a concave utility function.

concepts.title: St Petersburg game
concepts.summary: A coin is tossed until the first head; if that is on toss n the prize is 2^n. Its expected value is unbounded, yet few would pay much to play.

concepts.title: Utility
concepts.summary: A number on a scale such that the chooser prefers the gamble with the larger expected utility.

concepts.title: Diminishing marginal utility
concepts.summary: Each extra unit of money adds less utility than the one before, so the utility curve is concave.

misconceptions: Treating utility as a measure of happiness; in decision theory it is a number that represents the chooser's preferences over gambles.
Believing the St Petersburg paradox means the maths of expectation is wrong, when it shows that money is the wrong thing to average.
Thinking a concave utility makes someone irrational.
sequence: Pose the game and compute the first few terms of the expectation: each is (1/2)^n × 2^n = 1.
Observe the sum grows without limit, and note that a cap of N tosses gives an expectation of N.
Introduce Bernoulli's response: value the outcome by what it adds to wealth, with each extra dollar worth less.
Use u(x) = √x and compute expected utility for a gamble and for a sure amount.
State the rule: choose the option with the highest expected utility; the utility function carries the attitude to risk.
examples: Cap at 10 tosses: EV = 10 terms of 1 = 10. Gamble: 50% of 16, 50% of 64, with u = √x: expected utility = 0.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 8 = 6. Sure 36 has utility 6, so 36 is exactly as good as the gamble. Gamble 50% of 0 and 50% of 100: EU = 5. Sure 30 has utility √30 ≈ 5.48, so the sure amount is preferred though its value (30) is less than the gamble's EV (50).

figures.shows: The curve u(x) = √x with the chord between two outcomes; the sure-amount point on the curve is hidden until the learner places it.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a sure amount along the x axis until its utility equals the gamble's expected utility.

questionPlan.sample: With u(x) = √x, a gamble pays 16 or 64 with equal probability. What is its expected utility?
A St Petersburg game is capped at 10 tosses. What is its expected prize?
u(x) = √x. Gamble: 50% of 0, 50% of 100. Which is preferred, the gamble or a sure 30?

historyNotes: Nicolaus Bernoulli posed the problem in a letter of 1713; Daniel Bernoulli published his solution, with utility growing as the logarithm of wealth, in 1738 in the proceedings of the St Petersburg academy (see unverified).

lessons.title: Risk attitudes and certainty equivalents
lessons.objective: Compute a certainty equivalent and risk premium and say whether a utility function is risk averse, neutral or seeking.

concepts.title: Certainty equivalent
concepts.summary: The sure amount with the same utility as the gamble.

concepts.title: Risk premium
concepts.summary: The gamble's expected value minus its certainty equivalent.

concepts.title: Risk attitude
concepts.summary: Averse if utility is concave, neutral if linear, seeking if convex.

misconceptions: Equating risk aversion with refusing every gamble; a risk-averse chooser accepts a gamble if the price is low enough.
Reading the risk premium as an amount lost; it is the most the chooser would give up to avoid the risk.
Reading the shape of the curve backwards: a concave curve means averse, not seeking.
sequence: Reuse the gamble from the last lesson and read the sure amount with the same utility off the curve.
Define the certainty equivalent and the risk premium for the √x chooser: EV 40, CE 36, premium 4.
Show the three shapes of curve and what each does to the CE.
Apply to insurance: the maximum premium a risk-averse owner would pay exceeds the expected loss.
Note that what is risk-averse is about the curve, so changing the stakes changes the behaviour.
examples: u = √x, gamble 16 or 64 with equal chance: EU 6, CE = 6² = 36, EV = 40, risk premium 4. Convex u = x², gamble 0 or 10 with equal chance: EU = 50, CE = √50 ≈ 7.07, above the EV of 5, so the chooser is risk seeking. Insurance: wealth 100, 10% chance of losing 50, u = √w. EU without insurance = 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × √50 ≈ 9.707; CE ≈ 94.23 (since 9.707² ≈ 94.23), EV = 95, so the owner would pay up to about 5.77 against an expected loss of 5.

figures.shows: Three utility curves (concave, linear, convex) over the same range with the same two-outcome gamble chord drawn on each.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the gamble's probability slider and read where each curve's certainty equivalent falls relative to the EV.

questionPlan.sample: u(x) = √x and a 50/50 gamble between 16 and 64. What is the certainty equivalent?
Same gamble: what is the risk premium?
u(x) = x². A 50/50 gamble on 0 or 10 has a certainty equivalent of about 7.07. Which attitude is this?

lessons.title: Updating beliefs with Bayes' rule
lessons.objective: Revise a probability after a test result using natural frequencies and Bayes' rule, including a second independent result.

concepts.title: Prior
concepts.summary: The probability of a hypothesis before the new evidence.

concepts.title: Likelihood
concepts.summary: The probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is true.

concepts.title: Posterior
concepts.summary: The probability of the hypothesis after the evidence: P(H|E) = P(E|H) P(H) / P(E).

misconceptions: Treating P(positive | disease) as P(disease | positive), the transposed conditional.
Ignoring the prior (base rate), so that a 90% accurate test seems to mean a 90% chance of disease.
Adding the likelihoods of two tests instead of multiplying odds.
sequence: Pose the test question: prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 9%. What is the chance of disease after a positive result?
Do it with 10,000 people to make the counts concrete: 100 diseased, 90 test positive; 9,900 healthy, 891 test positive.
Read off 90 out of 981 positives, about 9.2%.
Turn the counts into the rule with the formula and name the three parts.
Update again with a second independent positive using odds and a likelihood ratio.
examples: 10,000 people: 90 true positives and 891 false positives, so P(disease | +) = 90/981 ≈ 0.0917. Spam: 20% of mail is spam, 'prize' is in 60% of spam and 3% of other mail: P(spam | prize) = 0.12/(0.12 + 0.024) = 5/6. Second positive: odds 90:891 times likelihood ratio 0.9/0.09 = 10 gives 900:891, so P = 900/1791 ≈ 0.5025.

figures.shows: A bayes_table for the test: counts of people by true state and test result. The posterior cell is hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Set prevalence, sensitivity and false-positive rate with sliders, then fill in the posterior.

questionPlan.sample: Prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 9%. Out of 10,000 people, how many test positive in total?
With the same test, what is the probability of disease after one positive result, as a percentage to one decimal place?
20% of mail is spam. 'Prize' appears in 60% of spam and 3% of other mail. What is P(spam | 'prize'), to two decimal places?

lessons.title: What perfect information is worth
lessons.objective: Compute the expected value of perfect information and use it as the ceiling on what to pay for any information.

concepts.title: Expected value of perfect information
concepts.summary: Expected value of choosing after learning the state, minus expected value of the best choice now.

concepts.title: Value of the best choice now
concepts.summary: The highest expected value among the options before any information arrives.

misconceptions: Thinking information is worth its accuracy and not the decisions it changes; if it would never change the choice it is worth nothing.
Paying for information about a state that does not affect the payoffs.
Confusing EVPI (an upper limit) with the price of a real, imperfect test.
sequence: Take an invest-or-not project: success has probability 0.4 and pays 100, failure 0.6 and loses 30, not investing pays 0.
Compute the best choice now: investing, with EV 0.4 × 100 - 0.6 × 30 = 22.
Imagine a seer who tells you the state first: invest only on success, so EV is 0.4 × 100 + 0.6 × 0 = 40.
Subtract: EVPI = 40 - 22 = 18.
Show the same number as expected regret of the best choice now (0.6 × 30) and state that no real information can be worth more.
examples: Project: EV invest = 22; EV with a perfect forecast = 40; EVPI = 18. Expected regret of investing is 0.6 × 30 = 18. A consultant offering a 'guaranteed' forecast for 25 is overpriced; one for 12 is worth the money.

figures.shows: Two side-by-side trees: choose then learn the state, and learn the state then choose. Values are blank.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the value of each tree and read the difference.
figures.placement: The ceiling on the price of information.

questionPlan.sample: Investing pays 100 with probability 0.4 and loses 30 with probability 0.6; not investing pays 0. What is the expected value of the best choice now?
What is the expected value of perfect information for this project?
A forecast service charges 25 for a perfect forecast of this project. What should you do?

historyNotes: The expected value of information was formalised by Ronald Howard in 1966 (see unverified).

lessons.title: Paying for a test
lessons.objective: Use Bayes' rule inside a decision tree to find the expected value of sample information and decide whether a test is worth its cost.

concepts.title: Expected value of sample information
concepts.summary: Expected value of choosing after a real, imperfect test, minus expected value of the best choice now.

concepts.title: Pre-test and post-test
concepts.summary: Before the test you only have probabilities of each result; after it you use the posterior to choose.

misconceptions: Using the test's accuracy as the probability of success; the posterior also depends on the prior.
Forgetting that you only buy information if it can change the decision; a test that leaves the choice unchanged has an EVSI of zero.
Adding the test cost to the payoffs of only one branch.
sequence: Same project: a test says 'good' 80% of the time when it will succeed and 30% of the time when it will fail.
Posterior after good: 0.32/0.5 = 0.64. After bad: 0.08/0.5 = 0.16.
Choose after each: invest after good (EV 53.2), do not invest after bad (invest would give -9.2).
Weight by P(result): 0.5 × 53.2 + 0.5 × 0 = 26.6. EVSI = 26.6 - 22 = 4.6, below EVPI of 18.

figures.shows: The two-stage tree: test, then decide, with branch probabilities from the table and the node values hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in each posterior, then each decision, then the test node.

questionPlan.sample: P(success) = 0.4; the test says good with probability 0.8 given success and 0.3 given failure. What is P(test says good)?
What is the probability of success given a good result?
What is the expected value of sample information for this test? Use best choice now = 22 and value with the test = 26.6.
The test costs 5. Should you buy it?

lessons.title: The axioms and the Allais paradox
lessons.objective: State what an expected-utility maximiser must satisfy and show that a common pair of choices cannot be explained by any utility function.

concepts.title: Independence
concepts.summary: If you prefer gamble X to gamble Y, you still prefer a mixture of X and Z to the same mixture of Y and Z.

concepts.title: Transitivity
concepts.summary: If A is preferred to B and B to C then A is preferred to C.

concepts.title: Money pump
concepts.summary: Someone with cyclic preferences will pay a small fee for each trade round the cycle and end up where they began, poorer.

misconceptions: Believing a non-linear utility function makes a chooser break expected utility; the paradox is about probabilities, not curvature.
Assuming that a choice that feels sensible must be rational in this narrow sense.
Reading the paradox as showing people are foolish and not that the theory has a testable consequence.
sequence: State the axioms the theory needs in plain words: complete, transitive, continuous, independent.
Show how a cycle of preferences gives a money pump.
Set out Allais's choices: A is 1M for sure; B is 89% 1M, 10% 5M, 1% nothing. C is 11% 1M; D is 10% 5M.
Show that preferring A to B and D to C needs 0.11u(1M) greater than 0.10u(5M) + 0.01u(0) and also the reverse.
Say which axiom the common pattern breaks and what theorists do about it.
examples: A over B means 0.11u(1) > 0.10u(5) + 0.01u(0). C over D means 0.11u(1) > 0.10u(5) + 0.01u(0): the same inequality. So A over B together with D over C is impossible for any u. EV of B in millions: 0.89 × 1 + 0.10 × 5 = 1.39. Money pump: A over B over C over A, a fee of 1 per trade, three trades round the cycle cost 3.

figures.shows: The four gambles as probability bars over the three prizes (0, 1M, 5M), with the common 89% shaded in both pairs.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a gamble in each pair, then switch on the 'remove the common part' view.
figures.placement: Why the pairs are the same.

questionPlan.sample: Which axiom does the common A-and-D pattern violate (independence, transitivity or continuity)?
Someone prefers A to B, B to C and C to A, and pays 1 for each swap to the preferred item. How much do they pay after three swaps?
Gamble B pays 1M with probability 0.89, 5M with probability 0.10 and nothing otherwise. What is its expected value in millions?

historyNotes: Maurice Allais published the paradox in 1953; von Neumann and Morgenstern had set out the axioms in 1944 (see unverified).

lessons.title: Prospect theory, framing and sunk cost
lessons.objective: Use a reference-dependent value function to explain loss aversion and framing, and recognise sunk-cost reasoning.

concepts.title: Loss aversion
concepts.summary: A loss weighs more heavily than an equal gain.

concepts.title: Framing
concepts.summary: Describing the same outcomes as gains or as losses changes the choice.

concepts.title: Sunk cost
concepts.summary: Money already spent and gone whatever you now choose; it should not affect a forward-looking choice.

misconceptions: Treating framing effects as people misunderstanding the numbers; the numbers are identical and the choices still shift.
Reading sunk cost as 'never think about past spending'; past spending is relevant only through what it tells you about the future.
Treating the simple loss-aversion factor as a fixed law.
sequence: Present the disease-programme problem: 600 people at risk; save 200 for sure, or a one-in-three chance of saving all 600.
Show that the loss-framed version has the same expected result and that many people reverse their choice.
Introduce the value function: measured from a reference point, steeper for losses than gains.
Compute with a simple model where losses count twice: a 50/50 gamble of +100 or -60 has value -10.
Close on sunk costs with a ticket already bought for an event you no longer want to attend.
examples: Gain frame: A saves 200 for sure; B saves 600 with probability 1/3 and none with probability 2/3, so EV is 200 for both. Loss frame: C means 400 die; D means nobody dies with probability 1/3 and 600 die with probability 2/3, EV deaths 400 for both. Model v(gain) = x, v(loss) = 2x: 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × (-2 × 60) = 50 - 60 = -10, so the gamble is declined though its EV is +20. It would be accepted only if the win exceeded 120.

figures.shows: The same two programmes drawn twice as bar pairs, once labelled by lives saved and once by deaths; the shared outcomes are only revealed after both choices are made.
figures.learnerAction: Choose in each wording, then switch on the view that overlays the outcomes.

questionPlan.sample: Losses count twice as much as gains. A 50/50 gamble wins 100 or loses 60. What is its value under this model?
With the same model, what is the smallest win that makes a 50/50 gamble against a loss of 60 acceptable (value above zero)?
You paid 80 for a ticket you would now sooner skip; the event costs 30 in travel and is worth 20 to you. What does forward-looking reasoning say?
questionPlan.answer: Skip it: 30 exceeds 20 and the 80 is gone either way
choices: Skip it: 30 exceeds 20 and the 80 is gone either way

historyNotes: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory paper is 1979; the framing paper is 1981 (see unverified for the percentages).

lessons.title: When the state fights back
lessons.objective: Say what changes when the other side chooses, and find dominant strategies and equilibria in a two-by-two game.

concepts.title: Chooser vs player
concepts.summary: A state of the world does not react to your choice; another player does.

concepts.title: Dominant strategy
concepts.summary: A strategy that is best against everything the other player might do.

concepts.title: Nash equilibrium
concepts.summary: A pair of strategies where each is the best reply to the other.

misconceptions: Treating the other player as a random state with fixed probabilities, which ignores that they reason about you.
Believing that an equilibrium is the best outcome for both; in the prisoner's dilemma it is not.
Looking for a dominant strategy only for yourself.
sequence: Start from a decision under uncertainty where the 'state' is the other player's move, with a belief about what they will do.
Compute expected values of each of your options against that belief.
Replace the belief with a reason: what would they do if they also had payoffs to maximise?
Find the dominant strategy and equilibrium in the prisoner's dilemma.
Point to economics-markets-and-strategy for repeated games and to further reading.
examples: Opponent plays Left with probability 0.7. You choose Up (4 vs Left, 1 vs Right) or Down (2 vs Left, 3 vs Right). EV(Up) = 0.7 × 4 + 0.3 × 1 = 3.1; EV(Down) = 0.7 × 2 + 0.3 × 3 = 2.3. Prisoner's dilemma payoffs (you, other): both cooperate 3,3; you cooperate, other defects 0,5; you defect, other cooperates 5,0; both defect 1,1. Defect pays more than cooperate against either move (5 > 3 and 1 > 0), so it is dominant, and (defect, defect) is the equilibrium though (3,3) is better for both.

courseCheck: A mixed set: build and roll back a tree from a short scenario; choose by maximin and minimax regret; compute an expected utility, a certainty equivalent and a risk premium; apply Bayes' rule to a test; compute EVPI and EVSI and decide whether a test is worth its price; recognise an Allais-type inconsistency, a framing reversal and a sunk-cost argument; find a dominant strategy in a two-by-two game.
platformNeeds: decision_tree figure: nodes (decision square, chance circle, leaf), probabilities on branches, a learner roll-back mode in which the learner types each node value and the figure checks it, and a switch that hides or shows rolled-back values. The svg_figure fallback in lessons 3, 7 and 8 draws the tree statically with a table of node values beside it.
Utility explorer extension for graph_plot: a curve family (sqrt, log, linear, square) with a draggable gamble chord that reports EU, CE and risk premium.
Optional sensitivity slider: vary one probability and watch the chosen option switch at the break-even value.
unverified: The 1713 date of Nicolaus Bernoulli's letter to Montmort and the 1738 publication of Daniel Bernoulli's paper in the St Petersburg academy's Commentarii.
The 1944 date of von Neumann and Morgenstern's book, 1953 for Allais, 1979 for Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, 1981 for the Science framing paper.

The commonly reported choice percentages in the 1981 framing study (about 72% for the sure option in the gain frame and 78% for the risky option in the loss frame): quote only after checking the paper.
That the Allais figures used here (1M, 5M, 89/10/1) match the commonly taught modern version and not Allais's original francs; present them as 'a standard form'.
Ronald Howard 1966 as the origin of the expected-value-of-information formulation.
The dates and attribution of maximin (Wald) and minimax regret (Savage, 1951; Niehans 1948) and the principle of insufficient reason (Laplace).
A loss-aversion coefficient of 2 is a teaching simplification; published estimates vary (about 2.25 is often quoted from 1992): do not state it as a law.
All sources were unreachable from the research session (external hosts blocked), so every source is marked verified false.
